questions.question: Explain why the lesson calls ethics 'the precondition for the entire discipline' of Accounting, and how ethics and internal control work as 'two hands of the same grip'.
questions.expected_answer: Financial information only has value if it can be trusted; if records can be bent to convenience they stop being information. So every accounting principle assumes people willing to follow rules. Internal control makes dishonesty difficult; ethics makes it unwanted — controls alone fail against determined people, and culture alone fails with zero checks, so a business needs both.

questions.question: Name the seven characteristics of the code of ethics and give a one-line business example of any three.
questions.expected_answer: Leadership, discipline, transparency, accountability, fairness, sustainability, responsible management. Examples: leadership — the owner follows the same cash rules imposed on staff; accountability — the manager explains a loss rather than burying it; sustainability — refusing profit today that destroys the base of profit tomorrow (e.g. not dumping waste, not buying stolen stock).

questions.question: Describe the four-move method for an ethics scenario question and apply it briefly to: 'The owner tells the bookkeeper to leave some cash sales out of the records.'
questions.expected_answer: Move one, state the issue: sales are deliberately excluded to evade tax. Move two, name the characteristics: leadership (dishonesty instructed from the top), transparency and fairness breached. Move three, argue the link: records no longer show what happened; the unpaid tax burdens honest taxpayers. Move four, consequence and correction: penalties, prosecution and lost credibility follow; all sales must be recorded and the code applied from the owner downward.
